comments.author: SwellJoe
comments.text: I'm running the 14B in llama.cpp (a version from yesterday), the 8-bit quantization from bartowski, and it looped on variations of the same paragraph for five minutes before running out its turn budget, in response to a pretty simple chat request that other similar-sized models (e.g. Gemma 4 12B) have no trouble with, a web search and data summarization task, sort of the sweet spot for models this size. It's possible llama.cpp needs some update to work with this model, but it's based on Qwen 3, so I would expect it to be pretty well-supported. The chat template is the same one upstream ships, which may or may not be correct. I'm currently downloading the 16-bit version, to see if it's quantization pathology. I'm also not confident it knows what a CSV is, either, as it put the data into a Markdown table during its reasoning phase as an example of how to present the data (my prompt asks for data in a CSV). My experience with most Qwen fine-tunes is they get dumber, but their benchmark results suggest otherwise, so I have to assume it's a llama.cpp incompatibility. Edit: Same looping in BF16. So, probably have to wait on a llama.cpp update.

comments.author: amluto
comments.text: I wonder how this compares to going all-in: widen the input embedding to fit the output (post-“Hybrid Link”) latent vector and a token embedding and pass both through even when in text mode. After all, you’re paying essentially the full cost of running the latent-mode model while generating text, so why not let it latently reason at the same time? (Or just add the vectors instead of using wider vectors - everyone seems to have good results from munging vectors together with plain addition.)

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、Hybrid Reasoning Agentsの実際の動作と互換性についてで、特にllama.cppでの14Bモデルのループや量子化問題が指摘された点が最も多く取り上げられた。賛否両論としては、賛成側はQwen 3系への適用や、潜在空間での reasoning をテキスト生成と同時に行える可能性に期待し、否定的・懐疑的側は現在の実装がバグや効率の低さを露呈し、さらにチューニングやllama.cppのアップデートが必要だと指摘した。注目コメントとして、「入力埋め込みを拡張し、潜在ベクトルとトークンベクトルを常に併用（または単純加算）すれば、テキストモードでも潜在理由付けを同時に行えるのではないか」というアイデアが挙げられ、これによりコストを無駄にせず理由付け能力を向上させられるかという洞察が示された。
stories.editor_note: ハイブリッド推論エージェントは潜在空間で思考しテキストで行動する新枠組みで、推論コスト削減とマルチモーダル連携が期待され、国内のLLMスタートアップが注目している。

stories.title_en: Someone behind the software
stories.title_ja: ソフトウェアの陰にいる人

comments.author: jwr
comments.text: As a SaaS author, I couldn't agree more. That's how I see my work: the value is not in the code (AI can code better than me at this point), nor even in the software architecture (AI is just getting to the point where it will get better than me). It's in deciding what to build and what not to build, defining the overall character and vision of the product, looking at each screen and thinking "how does this help my customer do their job". This, unfortunately, takes time, as one has to restart many times because of ideas that turned out not to be as great as one had initially thought. And it results in software that is called "opinionated", and often does not follow what the "industry" does.

comments.author: allenu
comments.text: Something I've been thinking about a lot is that ultimately AI does not have values, intent, and taste. Even with humans, each of us has different values, intent, and taste, although we do share many of these things. As a living human being, you have biological or cultural desires and particular goals that you want to accomplish while you're alive on this earth. When you're creating art or even a product, what you create is a result of your particular values and particular tastes and those drive some sort of purpose for whatever it is you're creating. What you're building is, generally, made for the consumption or use by another person (even if indirectly), and we mostly have empathy and want those people to have a good experience with whatever we're creating. We think about our audience and weigh their particular needs. When you use good software, you can sense the intent in what was made. The person (or team) combined their particular point of view with that of the goals of the user. At this point, I don't think agentic coding is going to give you that, at least not fully. It might get most of the shared values and common things right as a result of its training data, but a human still needs to edit the output or steer it on a good path that only they can see and which is part of a larger vision. For simpler needs, taste and values matter less, but for more complex things, it makes a difference, in my opinion.

I just picked up “The mind of the Maker” by Sayers, which Fred Brooks cites in The Mythical Man Month: “ Dorothy Sayers, in her excellent book, The Mind of the Maker, divides creative activity into three stages: the idea, the implementation, and the interaction. A book, then, or a computer, or a program comes into existence first as an ideal construct, built outside time and space, but complete in the mind of the author.” He goes on to say how the user meets the mind of the maker in the interaction: “The creation is complete when someone reads the book, uses the computer, or runs the program, thereby interacting with the mind of the maker.”

The opinions are those of the creators and that isn’t changing with AI.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点：ソフトウェアの価値はコードやアーキテクチャではなく、「何を作るか・作らないか」を決める人間のビジョン、意図、味わいにあるという点。AIはコード生成はできるが、価値観や意図、味わいは持たず、人間が方向性を定め、意見の強い(opinionated)製品を形作る必要がある。また、シンプルなニーズでは味わいは重要でなくても、複雑な製品では人間の判断が差を生むという議論。  
賛否両論：多くのコメントは人間の意図が不可欠であることに賛同し、AIは共通の価値は学習データから近似できるが、最終的な方向付けや味わいは人間が編集・導く役割が残ると指摘。一方で、単純・機能的な要件についてはAIだけでも十分だとし、味わいの重要度はケースによるという意見も見られた。  
注目コメント：「Great software is opinioned」というフレーズを繰り返し挙げ、「The Mind of the Maker」におけるアイデア・実装・相互作用の三段階を引用し、ユーザーが作り手の意図に触れる瞬間を強調した洞察が特に注目された。
stories.editor_note: ソフトウェアの陰にいる人は、オープンソースプロジェクトの維持・サポートを担う無名のエンジニアたちを指し、彼らの貢献がサプライチェーンリスク低減に直結するという視点が新鮮だ。

comments.author: mikewarot
comments.text: I feel like we're reliving the late 1790s again, back then you had Ramsden figuring out how to divide the circle into into seconds of arc, taking the marking of scales from an artform into something that could be manufactured reliably. Maudslay with his thread cutting lathe took the making of screws from a manual process pawned off on apprentices to something that that could be done in mass production. Wilkinson's boring machine made it possible for Watt to build a pressurized steam engine. All of these tools are based on things that were one-offs of earlier efforts, and turned into practical machine tools by someone that history chose to remember. We're now at the point where making things by manipulating individual atoms is something a determined amateur can do, it's amazing! I find myself fascinated by the Wyler Inclinometer, which uses a thin copper disk with spiral arms as the basis of a differential capacitor, and when complete, resulting in a device that can used to calibrate a granite surface plate. It can typically measure 1 micron/meter of deviation. We now have 3d printers that can reliably make almost anything you want by fusing filament, or stereolithography, or fusion of metal powders. You can buy desktop 5 axis CNC machines. There are control systems available to let you build almost any type of machine tool you can imagine, in as many axis as you want. We've got software defined radio, cheap atomic clocks, transistors that can switch megawatts, all within reach of a hobbyist. What an amazing time to be alive.

comments.author: DoctorOetker
comments.text: I too would associate "Bouba" with the rounded and "Kiki" with the sharper figure, but to me this is just a relatively universal sense of continuity vs discontinuities: the local curvature is continuous for "Bouba", every point on the curve has a single tangent, which evolves continuously as you walk along this presented curve. For Kiki: the local curvature is discontinuous: at the inward or outward points, there are 2 tangents, so the tangent abruptly switches value when passing through this point when walking along the curve. similarly the "B"s in "Bouba" are voiced plosives, while the "K"s in "Kiki" are unvoiced plosives. I think people would similarily classify "Titi, Pipi, Touta, Poupa, Kouka" like "Kiki" but "Didi, Douda, Bibi, Gigi, Gouga" like "Bouba". The vowels are obviously voiced by the vocal chord carrier wave "voice". So when we pass through the unvoiced (T/P/K) plosives, we notice discontinuity like the discontinuously evolving tangents along the boundary curve of the figure. Obviously mammals like dogs have a concept of continuity, topology, distance, they might get spooked by "open" stairs, because they can see between the planks, etc. And when we hear voiced (D,B,G) plosives, the voice while muted still evolves continuously.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、ブーバ／キキ効果が単なる言語的連想ではなく、形状と音声のクロスモーダル対応によるものかという点だった。多くのコメントは、とがった形は打撃音（無声音破裂音）と、丸い形は柔らかい音（有声音破裂音）に対応し、これが犬やひよこにも見られることから、普遍的な知覚メカニズムだと指摘した。一方、音の連続性・不連続性と図形の曲率の関係を詳細に解説し、有声音＝ブーバ、無声音＝キキという音韻パターンを挙げた意見もあった。賛否の分かれ目は実験の信頼性で、一部は犬が所有者の非言語的サインに敏感であるため結果が偏ると批判し、一方で統計的に有意な効果があると擁護する声があった。特に注目されたのは、音韻の有声・無声と形状の連続・不連続を結びつけた洞察的コメントと、実験設計の盲点を指摘したコメントだった。
stories.editor_note: 犬がブーバ/キキ効果を示す研究は、人間以外の動物にも音象徴性があることを裏付け、日本のペットテック分野での音声インターフェース設計に新たな示唆を与える。

stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**  
コメントでは、有料検索APIのコストパフォーマンスが中心に議論されている。DeepSeekの「成功リクエスト1000件あたり$0.75」という価格設定について、自前でSearXNGベースのツール（searxng‑ai‑kitやoh‑my‑pi）を使えば無料で同等の機能が得られると指摘され、個人利用ではコスト削減の観点から自ホスト型が推奨されている。また、検索APIの将来価格について、SEOやエージェント駆動型検索の普及によりプロバイダーが利用者に報酬を払う「ネガティブ価格」になる可能性が予測されている。さらに、LLMの学習にソース情報を明示する「ソース認識トレーニング」への期待が示され、現状の有料検索サービスはGoogleが有料APIを提供していないために存在しているという指摘もあった。価格面では、Brave Search APIが$5/1000件、Kagi APIが$12/1000件と比較され、DeepSeekの提示価格が最も安価であることが強調された。

**賛否両論**  
- 有料APIのコストに対する賛同：価格が低く、手軽に利用できる点は評価された。  
- 自ホスト型ツールへの懐疑：セットアップやメンテナンスの手間、信頼性やスケーラビリティにおいて不安を示す声もあり、個人利用以外では有料APIの方が現実的だとの意見も見られた。  
- ネガティブ価格予測については、実現可能性に賛否が分かれ、実際に広告モデルやデータ独占が進めば起こり得ると楽観的に見る者と、ビジネスモデルとして成立しないと疑問を呈する者がいた。

**注目コメント**  
- 「SearXNGベースのキットは無料で同様の検索結果を取得でき、APIキー不要。個人利用ならコストゼロが最大の利点」というコメントは、自ホストソリューションの実用性を具体的に示しており、多くの読者に共感を呼んだ。  
- 「将来的には検索プロバイダーが利用者に報酬を支払うネガティブ価格になるかもしれない」という洞察は、検索ビジネスの変革可能性を示唆し、今後の市場動向について考えるきっかけとなった。  
- 「LLMにソース認識トレーニングを施せば、回答の根拠を明示でき、信頼性が向上する」という提案は、AIの透明性と説明可能性への期待を高める点で注目された。
stories.editor_note: DeepSeekの検索・取得APIが1000件あたり0.75ドルと安価であることは、大規模言語モデルへの外部知識供給を低コストで行えることを示し、日本のエンタープライズAI導入コスト削減に直結する。

comments.author: Merrill
comments.text: A 1983 review of this remarkable system for the Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers (IEEE) attributes no fewer than eight "firsts" to SIGSALY. They are as follows: 1) The first realization of enciphered telephony 2) The first quantized speech transmission 3) The first transmission of speech by Pulse Code Modulation (PCM) 4) The first use of companded PCM 5) The first examples of multilevel Frequency Shift Keying (FSK) 6) The first useful realization of speech bandwidth compression 7) The first use of FSK - FDM (Frequency Shift Keying-Frequency Division Multiplex) as a viable transmission method over a fading medium 8) The first use of a multilevel "eye pattern" to adjust the sampling intervals (a new, and important, instrumentation technique) From https://www.jproc.ca/crypto/sigsaly1.html I think that the relevant patents remained classified until 1975.

comments.author: Animats
comments.text: Here's the technical description, from NSA.[1] It was really an awful kludge. Today, you'd think, digitize audio into a bit stream, encrypt bitstream. That's not how it worked. It was somewhat similar to the older A-3 analog scrambler, which split up audio into a number of bands and rearranged them, changing the rearrangement occasionally. In SIGSALY, incoming audio was filtered out into 10 frequency bands. There was also a dominant pitch detector and a "hiss" detector for unvoiced content. That created 12 analog signals to encrypt. Those signals were much lower bandwidth than the original speech. The patent seems to indicate that the frequency band signals were merely encoded as above or below a threshold. Not a full A/D, just a 1-bit threshold. As late as 1973, people were still trying vocoder-like technologies, but it became easier to work on audio in the digital domain and that died out.[2] The keying system changed the key every 20ms. It's not clear from the description whether the digitization of the 12 signals was also one sample for 20ms, but it probably was. If you used the same key bits for more than one analog sample, that would create a vulnerability. It's a one time key system, and those only work against serious opposition if the key is only used once. See VENONA. The articles indicate that synchronizing the key stream, which was on phonograph records, was a huge synchronization headache. Keeping signals in sync was really hard, and was part of the curse of analog TV, with horizontal and vertical hold controls. What this looks like is a system which had to work regardless of cost. So it was put together out of known building blocks. Straight digitization of audio was probably considered, especially since Alec Reeves, who had demoed pulse code modulation in 1937, was involved. But it was a high-risk technology. They would have had to invent a good A/D converter and a decent modem, which would have added technical risk to the project. It's one of those systems of historical interest because it was too soon. You couldn't really do the job in the straightforward way, but it needed to be done, resulting in a magnificent kludge. [1] https://www.nsa.gov/portals/75/documents/about/cryptologic-h... [2] https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UfpUexWJqb4

But your domain name registrar? Pick them carefully, don’t skimp, and make sure they have good support. Because when things go pear-shaped, you really want to be able to actually talk to someone to change your web server or e-mail DNS records (or even DNS servers) to somewhere else. Big registrars can’t afford any support costs since they prefer to squeeze the price down as far as possible, and therefore they prefer to simply lose or outright drop any customer in case of any and all problems. A small registrar might also be so small as to know you personally, which will help monumentally against any social engineering attacks. comments.author: antasvara
comments.text: Nathan Fielder is pretty well-known for his work in The Rehearsal and Nathan for You. Nathan for You resides in the docu-comedy genre, where you take advantage of real people's reactions to absurd situations for comedic effect. Other examples are things like Kitchen Nightmares (where Gordon Ramsey goes into real restaurants and "fixes" them). It's a well-done version of the idea, but not revolutionary IMO. The Rehearsal, however, extends the idea further. In that show, he helps real people "rehearse" for hard conversations. It involves Fielder building extravagant sets and having absurdly detailed set-ups with multiple actors, then running the conversation multiple times. What makes this "different" is that now the real person is partially in on it? Like, they know that they're on a set. They know that this is a simulation. So the show is more "meta" than previous entries in the genre, opening up other avenues for humour. I say this because You Can See Everything is best understood as a further extension of those projects. Even the name indicates this, because by nature of a documentary, you can't see everything. You have a real person in Elizabeth Holmes, being interviewed by a person in Fielder that's known for his stunts taking advantage of "real people," where he watches fictionalized versions of Holmes with Holmes herself? Viewed in light of his previous projects, this feels like an extension of them. But even with that, I think the setup does allow you to see something real in Holmes. She also knows how people "want" to see her! So there's also a sort of meta-narrative there too, where you know Holmes is on her best behavior to try and dispel the narrative from those fictionalized TV characterizations. The fact that she comes off poorly in the documentary says something, even accounting for the fact that Fielder is trying to sell a narrative. It's a real mind game, but I think it's representative of Holmes because of that. She is going to jail for a fraud that amounts to a similar sort of mind game, she agrees to a documentary to show herself differently, but that documentary is also a mind game. Wild stuff.

stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**  
多くのコメントで取り上げられたのは、Haskell の kind システムが「型→型」レベルの抽象化を可能にし、それによってモナドやその他の代数構造を理解しやすくなるという点である。記事が kind システムをどのように説明しているか、そしてそれが実際にプログラミングに役立つかが議論の中心だった。

**賛否両論**  
賛成側は、kind システムを expose する言語（例えば Haskell や一部の拡張された Rust）は、高階抽象を自然に扱えるため、モナドやレンズなどの概念が直感的になるとしている。反対側は、記事が抽象的すぎて具体的なコード例が欠如しており、「抽象の土地」に閉じ込められているように感じられ、実際には C でも同じことをできるという KISS 原則に反すると指摘している。

**注目コメント**  
「依存型については、Rust や Haskell でも限られた形しか使えないが、それによってできること（例えば型レベルでの証明や不変量の保証）は非常に好きだ」という意見が特に洞察に富んでおり、kind システムと依存型の関連性についての考えを示していた。また、「モナドを説明する際の最初のハードルは『型→型』を抽象化できることを示すことだ」という指摘も、議論の要点としてよく挙げられていた。
stories.editor_note: HaskellのKindシステムは、型の型を扱う高度な抽象で、型安全なDSLやエフェクトシステム設計に不可欠であり、日本の関数型コミュニティが実務での活用事例を共有している。

comments.author: BoppreH
comments.text: If you're on Python and your problem is too big for a single regex, but too small for a full-blown parser like in the article, I can recommend the built-in re.Scanner[0]. It's a regex-based tokenizer[1] (so no recursive parsing) in the `re` module, that for reasons is completely missing from any official documentation. You give it a pattern for each token type, and a function to process each match, and you get back a list of processed tokens. Importantly, it processes the list in one pass and ensures the matches are contiguous, where a naive `re.findall` with capture groups will ignore unmatched characters. You also get a reference to the running scanner, so you can record the location of the match for reporting errors. import re # Initialize the scanner. scanner = re.Scanner([ (r"\d+", lambda scanner, token: ('COUNT', int(token))), (r"\w+", lambda scanner, token: ('ANIMAL', token.removesuffix('s'))), (r"[,. ]", None), # None -> skip token. ]) # Scan a sample string. results, remainder = scanner.scan("45 pigeons, 23 cows, 11 spiders.") # Ensure we parsed the whole thing. assert not remainder print(results) # [('COUNT', 45), # ('ANIMAL', 'pigeon'), # ('COUNT', 23), # ('ANIMAL', 'cow'), # ('COUNT', 11), # ('ANIMAL', 'spider')] [0]: https://stackoverflow.com/a/693818/252218 [1]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexical_analysis#Tokenization

comments.author: ArneCode
comments.text: I really like the animations, makes it intuitive to understand what is happening! One disadvantage that I think parser combinators have, for example compared to parser generator libraries (where the parser is generated from a seperate grammar file), is that you have to add a lot of mapping / unwrapping code. In my opinion this makes the parsers harder to read. As an attempt to improve this, I have been working on a parser combinator library in rust. It adds two extra combinators (capture and bind) which can store the results of parsers in buckets (bind) and use the values stored in these buckets later to construct results (capture). This allows you to eliminate the unwrapping / mapping code and seperate the grammar from the result contstruction. If you have the time, I would really appreciate feedback on this! You can find it here: https://github.com/ArneCode/marser

comments.text: my technique to get a similar benefit is to write a quality PR description. a good PR description should be compact and helpful. describing something complex in a compact and approachable way requires understanding. the process of writing the description often leads me to understand hidden decisions the LLM made and occasionally uncovers bugs. my PR descriptions separately answer the following questions: Why is this change being made? a sentence or two about the problem, objective, etc, and a link to more detail (tickets, docs, etc) if available What does this change accomplish? typically describes observable changes, requirements, etc. crucially this section avoids describing how the change is implemented. the act of separating what from how isn't new, but it's crucial in the LLM era How does this change accomplish its goal? the answer to this question is "read the code", but the job of a PR description is to provide a quick hand drawn map before dumping the reviewer into the jungle. drawing a good "how" map requires understanding the jungle and the new path through it. the risk with LLMs (or any outsource) doing the work is the loss of understanding. this exercise encourages understanding.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、AIが生成したコードをそのままマージする前に人間が理解しているかを確認する「Sphinx」のような仕組みの有用性だ。多くのコメント者は、AIに頼りすぎると自分のスキルが伸びず、単にBigAIの訓練データを増やすだけになると指摘し、学習の機会を失うリスクを懸念した。一方で、PRボタンや「もう一人の人間の注意を引く前」にクイズを挟むことで無駄なレビューを減らせるという賛成意見もあり、コードレビューの質を向上させるゲートとして機能すると評価された。  

賛否の分かれ目は、クイズが学習促進になるか、あるいは単なる面倒な手続きになるかである。支持側は、質問を通じて実装の意図や設計判断を振り返る機会が得られると主張し、逆に批判側は、すでにPR説明書を丁寧に書くことで同様の理解を得られるとし、クイズは余計な負担だと考えた。  

注目コメントとして、PR説明書を「なぜ」「何を」「どう」の３つの質問に分けて書く手法を紹介し、これがLLM時代の「何を実装したか」と「どのように実装したか」を分離する重要な練習だと指摘した意見が挙げられた。また、半年前に同様のアイデアを実装したPEAK（Proof of Effort And Knowledge）というツールが紹介され、不正防止のためのアンチチート機能が組み込まれていたことが言及された。これらの議論から、AIコード生成時代における人間の理解をどう保証・深めるかが核心であることが浮かび上がった。
stories.editor_note: SphinxはAIコード出荷前にクイズを仕掛けるフックで、生成コードの品質保証を開発者自身に促し、日本のMLOpsチームが同様のセルフチェックパイプラインを導入し始めている。
